I have about two minutes before my next call, so start wherever you want. What is this?
Then let me start with how it works today. We used to run the auditions on paper, and honestly we still do. Four thousand videos, and a team of six would sit in a room for three weeks.
Three weeks. Is that the reading, or the waiting?
Mostly the waiting. The bottleneck is one person: nobody can start until she has watched everything. So the lead time is three weeks even when the work is four days.
Right. And you want money to fix it.
Not yet. I built a proof of concept on two weekends, for one category, with real videos. It is running. I would like you to watch it for four minutes, and then we talk about the budget.
That is the right order, and almost nobody does it. What does it cost me if I say yes?
One editor, two days a week, for one season. That is the trade-off: we lose him now and we get three weeks back every season after that. And I would roll it out beside the paper, not instead of it.
Somebody will push back and say the team will never use it. They said that about the last three things.
They are right to. That is why it runs beside the old one for a season: approval is not buy-in. Who has to sign off on it, apart from you?

I sit on the other side of the table, so let me tell you what happens in my head in the first thirty seconds. I am not listening for your idea. I am listening for whether you understand the thing you want me to change. If you open by telling me how the process works today, and you get it right, including the boring part that everyone forgets, then I relax, and everything after that lands differently. If you open with the solution, I spend the rest of the meeting checking whether you actually know the problem, and I stop hearing you. The second thing I listen for is what it costs me. Not money, necessarily. Time, attention, one person I would have to move off something else. Anybody who names that cost before I do has already won half the argument, because it means I am not going to find it later on my own. And the third thing, honestly, is whether you have thought about what happens when it does not work. Nobody signs off on something that has only one ending.

We used to run the auditions on paper, and I mean actual paper. Four thousand people would send a video, and a team of six would sit in a room for three weeks with printed sheets, and every one of those sheets had a name written by hand. It worked, in the sense that a shortlist came out at the end. But the lead time was three weeks, and the bottleneck was always the same: one person had to watch everything before anyone else could start. So I built a small version of a new system, for one category only, and I did not ask anybody for a budget. That was the whole trick. I built the proof of concept on two weekends, showed it running with real videos, and then asked for the money. The first answer was still no. Somebody pushed back and said the team would never use it, and that was a fair objection, so we ran it beside the paper for one season. That was four years ago. Nobody has printed a sheet since.
